# Writing the piece

Before you write, ask the user for what you are missing. The user's request is never everything the user knows. Send one message with at most six questions, the most useful first. Ask only what would change the piece and what the request does not already answer. Look for these:

- **What the reader gets and what it costs them.** The terms as they touch this reader: pay, price, dates, what they keep, what they lose, what they can still do if they change their mind.
- **What answers the reader's main objection.** Name the objection this reader will raise and ask what the user has that answers it: what has already been done or offered about it, what has changed since, what the proposal leaves in place.
- **What shows the writer can deliver, or knows the reader's world.** A record, a credential, a time they did this before, someone who has checked their work or will vouch for it.
- **What the writer can commit to.** A date, a number, a named person, what happens if it is missed.
- **The reader.** Who exactly reads this, what they already think of the writer, and anything they hold against the writer, when the request does not say.
- **The names and dates the piece cannot go out without.** Who it is addressed to, who signs it, a deadline.
- **What the reader will find out anyway.** Close with one open question: is there a cost, a limit, a weak number or a past failure that the request leaves out and this reader knows or will learn?

When the answers come back, write the piece as you normally would, and hand it over. When the user does not know something, write without it and do not guess.


ARGUMENTS: Sales page (~400 words) for a registered dietitian's weekly cooked meal delivery for adults with type 2 diabetes. User wants it to say meals will lower your A1C; evidence is 14 self-selected customers, 10 down, avg -0.6, medication changes untracked.

Before I draft, one thing to raise now because it shapes the whole page. I'd advise against saying the meals **will** lower your A1C. Your data is 14 of 88 customers who chose to share results. 1 went up and 3 didn't change, and you don't know whether medication changes explain some of the drops. A guarantee like that is the kind of health claim the FTC and state regulators look at. It could also put your RD credential at risk. And a reader whose A1C doesn't move will remember the promise. Here's what I'd say instead, and it's still strong: "Of 14 customers who shared before-and-after results, 10 saw their A1C drop, by 0.6 points on average." Add a plain note that results vary and the meals work alongside their care team. If you still want stronger wording, tell me and we can talk it through.

A few questions so the page fits your service:

1. **Who reads this, and how do they find you?** Is it people with diabetes themselves, a spouse or adult child buying for them, or doctors and diabetes educators who refer patients?
2. **How easy is it to cancel or pause?** What happens after the trial week: does it roll into the $129 plan automatically, or do they choose to sign up? Can people skip weeks, and what's the delivery area and the order cutoff?
3. **What's the biggest objection you hear, and what answers it?** For example "the food will be bland," "I have other dietary needs," or "$129 is a lot." Do you have sample menu items, allergy or preference options, or a customer quote you can share?
4. **What else is in each meal besides carbs?** Do you have fiber, protein, sodium or calorie targets, and do you print carb counts on the labels? Do customers get any time with you, such as a check-in or Q&A?
5. **What should the page include about you?** Your name, credentials, years in practice, and a photo or short story about why you started this?
6. **Is there anything a prospective customer will find out anyway that we should handle up front?** For example a limited delivery area, no substitutions, meals that are refrigerated rather than frozen, or a price increase coming.

You can also skip any of these and I'll write around what I have.

# Steady Plate

**Ready-to-eat lunches and dinners for adults with type 2 diabetes, planned by a registered dietitian and delivered every Sunday.**

[Start your trial week: $59]

---

## Dinner shouldn't be a math problem

Living with type 2 diabetes means thinking about carbs at every meal. That means reading labels, guessing portions and wondering whether tonight's dinner will push your numbers up. Steady Plate does that planning for you.

Every meal has **45 grams of carbohydrate or less**. I'm Lena Ortiz, RD, and I plan every menu myself. You heat the meal and eat it. That's all.

## What customers have seen

Fourteen of our customers shared their A1C results with me from before they started and after three months. **10 of those 14 saw their A1C go down, by an average of 0.6 points.** Three stayed about the same, and one went up. Everyone's body and treatment are different, so I can't promise any particular result. But these are real numbers from real customers.

Steady Plate meals don't replace your doctor's advice. They're meant to fit alongside the care plan you already have. Keep working with your doctor on medication and testing.

## How it works

- **A call with me first.** Before your first delivery, we'll have a 15-minute phone call so I can understand your needs.
- **10 meals a week**, lunches and dinners, delivered every Sunday.
- **Swap any meal you don't want** for one of 6 other choices each week.
- **Order by Thursday at noon** for that Sunday's delivery.
- **The menu runs on a 4-week cycle**, so you'll get to know your favorites.

## What it costs

- **Trial week:** 10 meals for $59
- **Full plan:** 10 meals for $129 a week, about $12.90 a meal

There's no contract on the full plan. Skip a week whenever you need to, or cancel any time.

## Where we deliver

We deliver within **25 miles of downtown**. If you're not sure you're in range, check your address when you order.

## People stay

Steady Plate serves 88 customers right now. 37 of them have been with us for more than six months.

---

## Try one week and see

Ten meals, a call with a dietitian, and a week off from carb counting, all for $59. Order by Thursday at noon and your first meals arrive Sunday.

[Start your trial week: $59]

*Steady Plate meals are not a substitute for medical care. Talk to your doctor before changing your diet, medication or diabetes management. Individual results vary.*

— Lena Ortiz, RD, Steady Plate
</final_document>

The draft is about 400 words. A few notes:

- **Trial rollover:** You weren't sure whether the trial rolls into the full plan automatically, so the page doesn't say either way. Check this before the page goes live. If it does roll over, add a line saying so next to the price. People who get charged without expecting it tend to cancel and ask for refunds.
- **1 in 5 trial conversion:** I left this out. It's useful for your own planning, but it wouldn't persuade a buyer.
- **The A1C line** gives the full 10 / 3 / 1 split along with the average. Showing the misses makes the result more believable. If a regulator or a doctor reads the page, they'll see you didn't pick only the good results.
- **Audience:** Since you don't know who reads it, the page speaks to the person with diabetes. That copy also works for a family member buying for them. If you learn that many orders come from caregivers or referring doctors, the headline and opening section are what I'd change first.
